transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, I didn't even really make this appointment for myself. It was the student health center on campus that basically made me come. I went in there—I think it was last Tuesday, or maybe Wednesday?—because I needed this standard medical clearance form signed so I can participate in these youth workshops. It's this really amazing program where we get to mentor kids, and I've been looking forward to doing it all semester, so I just went in for what I thought was a quick sign-off. 

But then they did the basic physical, and the nurse weighed me, and the doctor came in and made this absolute huge deal out of it. They told me they couldn't sign the form because they say my weight is too low to clear me for the workshops. They were looking at my chart and pointing out how the number has kept dropping since I started school, which... I mean, okay, maybe it has, but they were acting like it’s this massive crisis. 

To me, it just feels like exactly what happens when I’m really focused and busy. You know? I'm taking a heavy course load, I'm always studying or working on projects, and I just get really dialed in. It’s just what happens when you're a busy student. But they basically held my clearance hostage and sent me here, so... yeah. That's why I'm here. I just really need that form signed so I can do the workshops.
Are you afraid of gaining weight?

Afraid? I mean... I guess "afraid" doesn't really even begin to cover it. It's more like this absolute, overwhelming panic. Just the idea of the number on the scale going up, even by one single pound, it completely paralyzes me. I can't even describe the anxiety it gives me. 

Like, if I were to just go to the dining hall and sit down and eat a quote-unquote normal dinner with my roommates, or if I found out I ate something that was cooked with butter or extra oil... my heart starts racing just thinking about it. Because to me, it’s not just about the food or the weight itself, it’s about what it means. If I gain weight, it feels like all my hard work and focus is just gone. It honestly feels like everyone around me will look at me and instantly be able to see that I’ve completely lost my discipline. 

And I really pride myself on my discipline, you know? With my heavy course load, my projects, the youth workshops I want to do... I have to be disciplined to keep it all together. So the thought of just letting that go, of eating something with butter and letting my body get out of control... people notice that stuff. They notice when you let yourself go and stop trying. They'll just know I failed. So yeah, I guess I am terrified of it, because I just can't be that person who loses her grip on things.
Do you think your weight is currently too low?

I mean... no? Not really? I know that's what the student health center was saying, and I know people keep throwing around the word "dangerous" and looking at me with these really concerned expressions, but honestly, it just feels so incredibly exaggerated to me. Like, I get that there's a chart with a curve and a line, and my dot is below the line they want it to be on, but everyone's body is different, right? 

It just feels like they're trying to make my body into this massive problem when I'm literally just living my life. I'm just trying to stay sharp for school. When I eat less, I feel lighter, I feel more focused, I don't get that sluggish, heavy feeling that makes it impossible to study for hours on end. And I have to study for hours on end. I have two massive papers due before Thanksgiving, and if I get cleared for this workshop, I'll be dedicating at least ten hours a week to mentoring, plus the commute. I need that edge. 

So when they sit there and tell me I'm "too low," it's like... too low for what? Too low for their textbook? Because I'm functioning. I'm getting straight A's. I'm doing the work. It just feels like they're completely ignoring everything else about me and hyper-focusing on this one number, making it seem like I'm on the verge of collapsing when I'm actually just highly efficient right now. I just don't see it the way they do at all.
Do you think you would look fat even if you were at a normal weight?

I mean... I don't really know how to answer that, because what even is a "normal" weight, you know? Like, normal for who? Normal for the health center's little chart? Because if I were at the weight they think I should be at... I just... I don't know if I'd use the word "fat," exactly, but I know I would feel completely awful. I would feel heavy, and slow, and just... wrong. 

Like, right now, I feel like I'm exactly where I need to be to get everything done. I can feel my bones, and I know exactly where my body is in space, and it just feels right. It feels tight and controlled. If I were at that heavier weight they want me at, I just know my clothes wouldn't fit the same, and I'd feel it every time I moved, every time I sat down in a lecture hall or walked across campus. I'd feel all this extra... just, excess. And I can't stand the thought of having excess anything right now. I don't have excess time, I don't have excess energy to waste, so why should I have excess on my body? 

So, I don't know if I'd look in the mirror and literally see the word "fat" flashing in neon lights, but I know I would look at myself and see someone who gave up. I would see someone who compromised and let herself get soft. And I just... I can't do that. I can't be that person. I don't even like thinking about what I would look like if I gained that weight, because it just makes my skin crawl. It's not even just about the aesthetic, it's about the feeling of it. Does that make sense? I just... I don't think I could handle looking at myself if I let my body get to that so-called "normal" place.
Do you ever eat an amount of food that you consider excessive in a short period of time?

Excessive? Um... no. No, definitely not. I mean, I don't even really know how someone would do that, to be honest. The idea of just sitting down and eating a huge amount of food all at once... it just doesn't compute for me. Like, I have my routine, you know? I know exactly what I'm going to have, when I'm going to have it, and exactly how much it is. It's all planned out. 

Like, for example, yesterday, I had my coffee before my 8 AM seminar, and then I had this tiny little container of blueberries that I portioned out the night before—exactly a quarter cup—and I ate that around 11:30 when I had a break between classes, and then... well, you get the idea. It's very structured. If I were to just suddenly eat a whole bunch of food, it would throw off the entire schedule, the entire balance of my day. And I can't afford to be thrown off balance right now. 

I see people in the dining hall sometimes, and they'll just have these massive plates piled high with pasta, and pizza, and then they go back for dessert, and they eat it all in like, twenty minutes. And I just sit there and watch them, and I literally cannot fathom how they do it. Doesn't it hurt? Doesn't it make them feel completely exhausted and sick? If I ate even a fraction of that, I wouldn't be able to study for the rest of the night. I'd just be sitting in the library feeling my stomach stretch and digest, and that's so distracting. 

So no, I don't ever do that. I don't think I've eaten an excessive amount of food in... I don't even know how long. Years, maybe? I just stick to what I know I need to keep going. It's precise. It has to be precise. If I just started eating excessively, everything else would just fall apart.
Have you had a regular menstrual period recently?

My period? Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by "recently." Because I haven't had one in... wow, I don't even know. A really long time. Honestly, it's been kind of a relief, if I'm being totally transparent. Because getting your period when you're trying to manage a full course load and extracurriculars and everything else is just... it's such a hassle. 

I remember when I used to get it, it was just this awful disruption. Like, I'd get cramps, and I'd feel so bloated and sluggish, and it would completely ruin my focus. I'd have to sit in a three-hour seminar just feeling terrible, and I couldn't concentrate on the material at all. And then there's the whole logistical nightmare of dealing with it when you're running back and forth across campus, trying to squeeze in library time between classes. It just felt like this massive, unnecessary burden that my body was forcing on me every month. 

So when it stopped, it was honestly like... one less thing to worry about. It just felt like my body was finally getting on board with my schedule, you know? Like it realized, "Okay, we don't have time for this right now, let's just shut this down so we can focus on what's important." It feels efficient. Like everything else I'm doing. It's just my body streamlining itself so I can keep up with everything I need to do. 

I know the health center made a big deal about it when I told them, but I just don't see why it's such a crisis. I'm not trying to have a baby right now. I'm nineteen. I'm a sophomore in college. I'm trying to get into this mentoring workshop and write these two massive papers. Why do I need to be menstruating to do that? If anything, not having it just proves that my body is adapting perfectly to the demands I'm placing on it. It's focused. It's not wasting energy on things I don't need. So no, I haven't had one, but I really, really don't see it as a problem. It's actually been incredibly convenient.
Do you ever feel like you've lost control while you're eating?

Lost control? No... no, definitely not. Honestly, the idea of losing control while eating is just... it's terrifying to even think about. I am always, always in control. That's kind of the whole point, isn't it? Like, if I lose control of that, what else falls apart? 

I was just talking to my roommate about something like this the other day—well, not this exactly, but she was complaining about how she stress-eats when we have midterms. She was telling me how she'll just open a bag of chips while reading her sociology textbook, and suddenly the whole bag is gone, and she doesn't even remember eating it. She called it "zoning out." And I just sat there looking at her like she had two heads. Because I cannot even comprehend how your brain allows you to do that. How do you just... zone out? How do you not know exactly what is going into your body at every given second? 

For me, eating is... it requires my full, absolute attention. It's a conscious, deliberate decision every single time. I know exactly what I'm doing. I know the exact weight of the apple slices I put in my little Tupperware container, I know exactly what time I'm allowed to open it, and I know exactly how I'm going to eat it. It's like... it's like a math equation. You don't just lose control in the middle of solving a calculus problem, you know? You have to follow the steps. You have to be precise. If I were to just snap and start eating without thinking, without measuring and planning, I would feel this overwhelming, suffocating panic. 

My whole life right now is about keeping everything tightly managed. The mentoring workshop applications, the papers, the reading assignments... I have a color-coded planner that dictates my entire week down to the fifteen-minute mark. Eating is just another part of that grid. It has to be. So, losing control? No. I've never felt that way. I feel the exact opposite. I feel so hyper-aware and so dialed in that sometimes it's exhausting, but it's a good kind of exhausting. It's the kind of exhausting that means I'm doing it right. I'm steering the ship. I would never just let go of the wheel like that, especially not with food. It just... it goes against every single fiber of how I operate.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is related to how you think you would look, or is it more about how you would feel?

I mean... I think it’s both? Or, like, they are so intertwined at this point that I can’t really separate them anymore. Because how I look completely dictates how I feel about myself as a person. It's not just about vanity or wanting to look like a model or something superficial like that. It's way deeper than that. 

Like, okay, for example... we had this showcase recently for one of my programs. It was a really big deal, lots of faculty there, we had all our work displayed, and I was so stressed leading up to it. The university photographer was there taking pictures of everyone standing next to their presentations. And when they emailed the link to the photo gallery out a few days later... I realized exactly how my brain works with this stuff. 

Because when I look at photos from the showcase, I don’t really see the artwork first. I don't even look at my own project, the one I literally spent weeks researching and formatting. I just immediately, instinctively, zoom right in on myself. Specifically, I zoom in on my arms and my waist. I scrutinize every single pixel to see how my clothes are hanging on me, how my arms look when they're just resting at my sides, how much space I'm taking up in the frame compared to the people standing next to me. 

And... if I look small enough in those pictures, I get this immense wave of relief. Because looking small means I feel like I’m serious and put-together. It's like visual proof that I am disciplined. If my waist looks tiny, it means I'm doing everything right. It means I'm a person who has her life completely under control, someone who is dedicated and focused. 

If I were to gain weight, and I looked at a photo and saw that my arms were bigger or my clothes were tight... I wouldn't just feel bad about my appearance. I would feel like a complete and utter failure. I'd feel sloppy. I'd feel lazy, like I let my guard down, like everything I've been working so hard for is just a joke. So the fear of gaining weight... it's the fear of losing that identity. My shape is basically the physical evidence of my work ethic. Does that make sense? The physical smallness is what allows me to feel mentally sharp and capable. I can't be a serious student, or a serious person, if I take up too much space. The space I take up has to be minimal so I can focus all my energy on my actual goals. So yeah, checking those showcase photos... it's just a constant metric for me to make sure I'm still that put-together person.
Have you ever eaten in secret?

In secret? Um, no. No, I don't think I've ever done that. I mean, hiding food or sneaking around to eat implies that you're ashamed of what you're doing, right? Like you're doing something wrong and you don't want anyone to catch you. But I'm not doing anything wrong. If anything, I'm doing everything exactly the way I'm supposed to. So there’s just... there's no reason for me to hide it. 

Like, if I’m at the library with my study group, and it’s time for my scheduled snack—which is usually just, you know, a specific amount of almonds or a green apple that I’ve already pre-sliced—I’ll just take it out and eat it right there at the table. I don't go hide in a bathroom stall or sneak off to my dorm room. I just eat it. Sometimes people will make comments, like, "Oh, is that all you're having?" or "You eat like a bird," but it doesn't bother me. I just tell them that eating a heavy meal makes me sluggish and I need to stay sharp for whatever we're working on. Which is completely true! I don't see why I should have to conceal my discipline. 

I actually think eating in secret would feel... I don't know, it would feel really chaotic to me. It goes back to that whole idea of losing control that you asked about earlier. People who eat in secret, like, they're usually the ones who are embarrassed because they're eating things they know they shouldn't, or they're eating massive amounts of it. Like my roommate and her stress-eating. She’ll sometimes hide her candy wrappers in the bottom of the trash can so I won't see them, which I always notice anyway, but... I just can't relate to that mindset at all. 

Everything I do is so calculated and intentional. I have my plan written out in my notebook, right next to my assignment deadlines and my workshop meetings. I leave it open on my desk. I don't care who sees it. It's just data. It's just a record of my efficiency. If I were to start hiding when I eat or what I eat, it would feel like I was undermining my own system. It would feel sneaky and messy, and I really, really don't do messy. Everything in my life has to be completely transparent and accounted for, so... no. I definitely don't eat in secret. There's just no need to.
Have you ever eaten a large amount of food in a short period of time?

A large amount? Oh, wow, no. No, never. I mean, honestly, I don't even think my body could physically handle that at this point, even if I wanted to, which I definitely don't. Because, like I was saying before about the apple slices and my Tupperware, everything I eat is so precisely portioned out beforehand. It's all measured. 

Like, if I'm making a salad for dinner, I don't just grab handfuls of greens and dump them in a bowl. I measure the exact amount of spinach—usually exactly two cups, pressed down just right into the measuring cup so the volume is exactly the same every time—and then I take my cherry tomatoes and I cut them into quarters. Not halves, but quarters, because it takes longer to eat that way, and I have to be very deliberate about it. And I eat very, very slowly. I put my fork down between every single bite. I chew everything completely before I even think about picking the fork back up. 

So the idea of eating a large amount of food, and especially doing it quickly in a short period of time? That's just completely alien to me. It sounds so chaotic and just... rushed. It sounds like a total loss of control, which, you know, we already talked about how much that terrifies me. I can't even imagine just putting food into my mouth without thinking about it or registering every single detail of what it is and how it fits into my daily allotment. 

Plus, if I eat too fast, or if I eat even a fraction more than what I had scheduled in my planner, I get this horrible, heavy feeling. It's like my whole body is weighed down with lead, and my brain gets all foggy, and I can't focus on my work. And I have so much reading for my political science seminar this week, I literally cannot afford to feel sluggish or distracted. Everything has to stay light and efficient. So no, I've never done that. I just... I couldn't. It goes against every single rule I have for how I operate.
Have you ever experienced episodes where you felt like you were eating much more quickly than usual?

Quickly? No, never. Like I was just saying, I actually do the exact opposite. I am so incredibly careful to make sure I am *not* eating quickly. 

Because if I eat quickly, it means I'm not paying attention, and I have to pay attention to every single bite. Like, if I have my scheduled apple—the green one I mentioned earlier—I don't just bite into it like a normal person might. I slice it paper-thin. And I have this rule where a meal or a snack has to last a specific amount of time. Usually, it has to take me at least thirty to forty-five minutes to finish, even if it's just a tiny amount of food. I literally watch the clock on my phone or the one on the library wall to pace myself. 

I think if I were to eat quickly, it would just feel like this chaotic blur. It would feel like I wasn't present, and I need to be completely present and aware of every single thing I'm consuming. My roommate, for example, she'll just inhale a bagel on her way out the door to her chem lab, literally walking down the hallway chewing and talking at the same time, and I just watch her and think... how can you even register what you just did? How does your body even process that? It honestly gives me anxiety just watching people eat fast like that. It’s so mindless. 

So, no, I never have episodes where I eat faster than usual. My "usual" is incredibly, incredibly slow. I'll sit in the dining hall with my notebook open, and I'll read an entire chapter for my seminar between bites. Entire groups of people will come, sit down, eat their heavy meals, and leave, and I'll still be sitting there with the same little bowl of quartered tomatoes. Because if I speed up, I lose the structure. And if I lose the structure, I lose my focus, and I start to feel out of control. So speed is just... it's completely out of the question for me. I have to draw it out as long as physically possible.
Have you ever made yourself vomit after eating?

Vomit? Oh, no. God, no. Just the thought of that is... no. That completely goes back to the whole "messy" thing I was talking about earlier. Making yourself throw up is so incredibly chaotic and, honestly, it just seems so desperate. Like, if someone is doing that, it means they’ve already messed up their plan, right? They ate something they weren't supposed to, or they lost control and ate too much, and now they're panicking and trying to physically undo it. But I never, ever put myself in a position where I need to undo anything, because my intake is already perfectly calculated beforehand. There are no mistakes to erase. 

And physically, it just sounds horrific. It’s a total loss of bodily control. My body is a machine, and I run it on very specific, very clean fuel. The idea of violently reversing that process... it just doesn't fit into my system at all. Plus, it's so inefficient. I've read about what it does to your body—it ruins your teeth, it messes up your throat, it makes your face all swollen and puffy. I can't have my throat hurting when I have to participate in my seminars. I have a huge presentation in my political science class next Tuesday, and my voice needs to be perfectly clear. I have to be sharp. I can't be dealing with the physical aftermath of something so destructive. 

It just seems like a frantic reaction, and I am never frantic. I am always completely in control of what goes in, so I never, ever have to worry about forcing it out. It just wouldn't make any logical sense for me to do something like that. So, no, absolutely not. Never.
Have you ever used laxatives or diuretics to help control your weight?

Laxatives? Diuretics? No, definitely not. That... that falls into the exact same category as throwing up, in my mind. It's just another way of trying to cheat the system after you've already failed, you know? Like, if you have to resort to taking pills to force your body to flush things out, it means you didn't have the discipline to restrict what went in in the first place. And discipline is literally the foundation of my entire routine. 

Plus, taking a pill to make yourself go to the bathroom... it just sounds so unpredictable. And I cannot handle unpredictability. What if it hits you when you're in the middle of a lecture? Or when I'm studying in the quiet section of the library? I practically live on the fourth floor of the library right now because I have two huge papers due before midterms, and I have this one specific carrel by the window that I always use. I can't be running back and forth to the bathroom, worrying about when a laxative is going to kick in. That would completely ruin my focus. I need to be able to sit there for four, five, six hours at a time without any interruptions. 

And diuretics... that's just messing with your water weight, right? It's fake. It's a temporary fix. It doesn't actually mean you've achieved anything real. My whole process is about real, measurable results based on pure control and restriction. I don't need artificial shortcuts. If I feel like I'm retaining water, or if I feel "heavy"—which, like I said, only happens if I somehow miscalculate, which is incredibly rare—I just adjust my water intake very carefully and maybe increase my walking time between classes. I don't take chemicals to force my body to do something. 

My body is supposed to be clean. It's supposed to be empty and efficient. Putting a bunch of harsh pharmacy pills into my system just feels toxic. It feels dirty. It would completely disrupt the purity of what I'm doing. So, no, I would never use anything like that. I don't need them because I don't make the kind of mistakes that would require them. I just stick to my plan. It's safer that way. It's the only way that makes sense.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight in a short period of time?

Well, I mean, I don't really see it as this huge, dramatic drop like people are making it out to be. The entire reason I'm even sitting here talking to you right now is actually because of the Student Health center. I had to go in for what I thought was just going to be a basic, five-minute physical clearance. I volunteer for these youth workshops—it's this program where we mentor high school kids, which is super important for my resume and I've spent weeks preparing my materials for it—and you have to get a medical sign-off to participate. I thought I’d just walk in, get the signature, and go right back to my study carrel. 

But they weighed me, and suddenly it was this massive ordeal. They literally refused to sign the form. Student health sent me here because they say my weight is too low to clear me for the youth workshops. Which is just... it's so incredibly frustrating because it completely disrupts my schedule and my plans. And yeah, they showed me my chart and made this big point about how the number has kept dropping, especially recently, but they were acting like it's some sort of emergency. 

To me, honestly? It just feels like what happens when I’m focused and busy. Like I was telling you, I’m taking advanced seminars, I have those massive papers due, I'm prepping for these workshops... I'm just operating at a very high level right now. When you have that much on your plate, and you're that dialed into your routine, you don't have time for excess. It's just a natural byproduct of being disciplined and staying focused on my goals. So, yes, I guess the number has gone down, and it's kept dropping, but it's not a problem. It's just efficiency. I don't understand why they can't just see that and sign my form so I can get back to my students.
Are there specific areas of your body where you're particularly concerned about gaining weight?

Well, I mean, it's not so much about gaining weight in one specific area, it's more about... it's about the overall shape and how it translates to, I guess, my presence? Like, okay, so last month, my art history seminar had this end-of-term showcase. It was a huge deal, all the faculty were there, and we had to present our final projects. I had been working on mine for literally weeks, pulling all-nighters, making sure every single detail was perfect. And of course, people were taking pictures the whole time. 

When I got the link to the photo gallery afterwards, I didn't even look at the artwork first. I know that sounds terrible, because I worked so hard on it, but I just... I couldn't. I immediately started zooming in on myself in every single picture. I was looking at my arms, checking to see how they looked against the dark fabric of my dress, and I was checking my waist, seeing if the belt was sitting right, if it looked sharp. And it's like... if I look at those pictures and I look small enough, if my arms look thin and my waist is completely defined and minimal, then I feel like, yes, I belong there. I feel like I look serious, you know? Like I'm a put-together, dedicated student who deserves to be taken seriously by the faculty. 

But if I were to see even a tiny bit of softness there, or if my arms looked even slightly wider than they should... it would completely invalidate everything. It would mean I wasn't disciplined enough. It would mean I was sloppy. And I can't be sloppy. So, yes, my arms and my waist are definitely the areas I fixate on the most, because they're the most visible indicators to me of whether I'm maintaining that level of strict control and professionalism. If those areas aren't perfectly tight and small, the whole image just falls apart.
Do you think your weight or body shape is abnormal even when others tell you it is not?

I mean, I hear what they’re saying. I’m not deaf. I know people keep saying it’s dangerous—like the nurses at Student Health, and even my mom when we FaceTime, they all use these huge, dramatic words like I'm on the brink of some absolute catastrophe. But honestly? It just feels so incredibly exaggerated to me. Like, completely blown out of proportion. 

They make it seem like my body is this massive problem that has to be fixed right this second, and they act like I'm completely irrational for not panicking along with them. But I’m literally just trying to stay sharp for school and my volunteer work. If I were to do what they want, if I were to just let go and let my body get soft and heavy, I would get so sluggish. I can’t afford to be sluggish. I have that huge paper due, I have the youth workshops I’m trying to get cleared for, I have my advanced seminars... I need that edge. I need to be completely dialed in. 

It’s like they don’t understand the pressure I’m under, you know? They just hyper-fixate on how I look or what the scale says, and they completely ignore the fact that my routine is exactly what allows me to manage a million things at once. My body isn't a problem, it's a tool. It's an efficient, finely-tuned tool that lets me do my work at the highest possible level. So when they tell me I look abnormal or that I'm in danger, I just... I can't even take it seriously. It just feels like they're making my body into this huge issue when I'm just doing what it takes to actually succeed and stay focused.
Do you think your body shape or weight is the way you perceive it to be, even if others see it differently?

I mean, I don't really know how to answer that because... well, I guess I just don't understand what you mean by "the way I perceive it" versus how others see it. Like, I'm the one living in this body, right? I'm the one who wakes up every single morning at 5:30 AM to go for my run before the campus even wakes up, and I'm the one who sits in the library for six hours straight, feeling my hip bones against the hard wooden chairs, knowing that I'm staying focused. I feel the reality of my body every single second of the day. 

When people tell me I look different than how I feel, or they try to say I'm not seeing myself clearly... it just doesn't make any sense to me. Like, how could I not see myself clearly? I look in the mirror, I check my arms, I check my waist, I see exactly what is there. I see the discipline. I see the results of all the hard work I put in. I don't know what they are seeing, but honestly, it feels like they are just projecting their own anxieties onto me. They see someone who is incredibly dedicated and maybe it makes them uncomfortable? I really don't know. But I know what I see, and I know what I feel, and I don't really get why everyone else's perception is supposed to be more accurate than my own when I'm the one actually doing the work and living this life.
Do you think your body shape is abnormal even when you look in the mirror and see that it looks normal?

I... I don't really know how to answer that either, honestly. Like, you're asking if I think it's abnormal when I look in the mirror and see it looks normal? But... I don't look in the mirror and see "normal." I don't even really know what "normal" is supposed to mean in this context. 

When I look in the mirror, I'm not looking for some generic standard of normalcy. I'm looking for... I'm looking for progress. I'm looking for the specific things I need to see to know I'm staying on track. Like, I have this full-length mirror in my dorm room—it's on the back of the closet door, the one I had to put up myself because the one they provided was warped and made everything look distorted—and every morning, right after I get back from my run and before I even shower, I stand there. I have a whole routine. I check the space between my thighs, I check the definition in my collarbones, I turn to the side to make sure my stomach is completely flat. 

I'm not looking at it and thinking, "Oh, this looks normal," or "This looks abnormal." I'm looking at it and thinking, "Okay, the collarbones are sharp today, that's good, that means the run worked," or "My stomach looks a little softer than yesterday, I need to be more careful with lunch." It's entirely about the metrics of my own discipline. So the idea of looking in the mirror and seeing "normal" and then thinking it's abnormal... it just doesn't compute for me. It's not about normal or abnormal. It's about whether I'm meeting my own standards, whether I'm maintaining the control I need to get through everything I have to do. If I meet those standards, then it's right. If I don't, then it's wrong. Normal doesn't even factor into it.
Do you think your body shape is acceptable to you, regardless of what others say?

I mean, acceptable? I guess so, as long as it looks the way I need it to look. Like, it’s not really about what other people think is acceptable, it’s about how I feel when I see myself in certain situations. But they weighed me, and suddenly it was this massive ordeal. They literally refused to sign the form. Student health sent me here because they say my weight is too low to clear me for the youth workshops. Which is just... it's so incredibly frustrating because it completely disrupts my schedule and my plans. And yeah, they showed me my chart and made this big point about how the number has kept dropping, especially recently, but they were acting like it's some sort of emergency. 

To me, honestly? It just feels like what happens when I’m focused and busy. Like I was telling you, I’m taking advanced seminars, I have those massive papers due, I'm prepping for these workshops... I'm just operating at a very high level right now. When you have that much on your plate, and you're that dialed into your routine, you don't have time for excess. It's just a natural byproduct of being disciplined and staying focused on my goals. So, yes, I guess the number has gone down, and it's kept dropping, but it's not a problem. It's just efficiency. I don't understand why they can't just see that and sign my form so I can get back to my students.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's restrictive eating patterns are driven by a desire to avoid weight gain specifically in certain parts of their body
doctor.question: Are there specific areas of your body where you're particularly concerned about gaining weight?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about specific areas of the body where the patient is concerned about weight gain, which directly corresponds to the body image and shape disturbance symptom where the patient focuses on their arms and waist.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean, it's not so much about gaining weight in one specific area, it's more about... it's about the overall shape and how it translates to, I guess, my presence? Like, okay, so last month, my art history seminar had this end-of-term showcase. It was a huge deal, all the faculty were there, and we had to present our final projects. I had been working on mine for literally weeks, pulling all-nighters, making sure every single detail was perfect. And of course, people were taking pictures the whole time. 

When I got the link to the photo gallery afterwards, I didn't even look at the artwork first. I know that sounds terrible, because I worked so hard on it, but I just... I couldn't. I immediately started zooming in on myself in every single picture. I was looking at my arms, checking to see how they looked against the dark fabric of my dress, and I was checking my waist, seeing if the belt was sitting right, if it looked sharp. And it's like... if I look at those pictures and I look small enough, if my arms look thin and my waist is completely defined and minimal, then I feel like, yes, I belong there. I feel like I look serious, you know? Like I'm a put-together, dedicated student who deserves to be taken seriously by the faculty. 

But if I were to see even a tiny bit of softness there, or if my arms looked even slightly wider than they should... it would completely invalidate everything. It would mean I wasn't disciplined enough. It would mean I was sloppy. And I can't be sloppy. So, yes, my arms and my waist are definitely the areas I fixate on the most, because they're the most visible indicators to me of whether I'm maintaining that level of strict control and professionalism. If those areas aren't perfectly tight and small, the whole image just falls apart.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think your weight or body shape is abnormal even when others tell you it is not?

target_item.name: Low_Weight_Severity_Non_Recognition
target_item.manifestation: I know people keep saying it’s dangerous, but it feels exaggerated to me, like they’re making my body the problem when I’m just trying to stay sharp for school and my work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a discrepancy between the patient's perception of their body/weight and others' perceptions. The patient's symptom S084 addresses this dynamic, specifically that others tell her the low weight is dangerous (abnormal), but she does not recognize the severity and thinks they are exaggerating.

patient.answer:
I mean, I hear what they’re saying. I’m not deaf. I know people keep saying it’s dangerous—like the nurses at Student Health, and even my mom when we FaceTime, they all use these huge, dramatic words like I'm on the brink of some absolute catastrophe. But honestly? It just feels so incredibly exaggerated to me. Like, completely blown out of proportion. 

They make it seem like my body is this massive problem that has to be fixed right this second, and they act like I'm completely irrational for not panicking along with them. But I’m literally just trying to stay sharp for school and my volunteer work. If I were to do what they want, if I were to just let go and let my body get soft and heavy, I would get so sluggish. I can’t afford to be sluggish. I have that huge paper due, I have the youth workshops I’m trying to get cleared for, I have my advanced seminars... I need that edge. I need to be completely dialed in. 

It’s like they don’t understand the pressure I’m under, you know? They just hyper-fixate on how I look or what the scale says, and they completely ignore the fact that my routine is exactly what allows me to manage a million things at once. My body isn't a problem, it's a tool. It's an efficient, finely-tuned tool that lets me do my work at the highest possible level. So when they tell me I look abnormal or that I'm in danger, I just... I can't even take it seriously. It just feels like they're making my body into this huge issue when I'm just doing what it takes to actually succeed and stay focused.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think your body shape or weight is the way you perceive it to be, even if others see it differently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about body image distortion (perceiving body weight or shape differently than others do). While my profile includes S046 (undue influence of weight/shape on self-evaluation) and S084 (non-recognition of low weight severity), it does not have a specific manifestation for experiencing body shape/weight differently from others.

patient.answer:
I mean, I don't really know how to answer that because... well, I guess I just don't understand what you mean by "the way I perceive it" versus how others see it. Like, I'm the one living in this body, right? I'm the one who wakes up every single morning at 5:30 AM to go for my run before the campus even wakes up, and I'm the one who sits in the library for six hours straight, feeling my hip bones against the hard wooden chairs, knowing that I'm staying focused. I feel the reality of my body every single second of the day. 

When people tell me I look different than how I feel, or they try to say I'm not seeing myself clearly... it just doesn't make any sense to me. Like, how could I not see myself clearly? I look in the mirror, I check my arms, I check my waist, I see exactly what is there. I see the discipline. I see the results of all the hard work I put in. I don't know what they are seeing, but honestly, it feels like they are just projecting their own anxieties onto me. They see someone who is incredibly dedicated and maybe it makes them uncomfortable? I really don't know. But I know what I see, and I know what I feel, and I don't really get why everyone else's perception is supposed to be more accurate than my own when I'm the one actually doing the work and living this life.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think your body shape is abnormal even when you look in the mirror and see that it looks normal?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about perceptual body image distortion (perceiving the body shape as abnormal even when seeing it looks normal). This is distinct from S046, which specifically covers the undue influence of body weight/shape on self-evaluation, and S084, which covers the lack of recognition of the severity of low weight.

patient.answer:
I... I don't really know how to answer that either, honestly. Like, you're asking if I think it's abnormal when I look in the mirror and see it looks normal? But... I don't look in the mirror and see "normal." I don't even really know what "normal" is supposed to mean in this context. 

When I look in the mirror, I'm not looking for some generic standard of normalcy. I'm looking for... I'm looking for progress. I'm looking for the specific things I need to see to know I'm staying on track. Like, I have this full-length mirror in my dorm room—it's on the back of the closet door, the one I had to put up myself because the one they provided was warped and made everything look distorted—and every morning, right after I get back from my run and before I even shower, I stand there. I have a whole routine. I check the space between my thighs, I check the definition in my collarbones, I turn to the side to make sure my stomach is completely flat. 

I'm not looking at it and thinking, "Oh, this looks normal," or "This looks abnormal." I'm looking at it and thinking, "Okay, the collarbones are sharp today, that's good, that means the run worked," or "My stomach looks a little softer than yesterday, I need to be more careful with lunch." It's entirely about the metrics of my own discipline. So the idea of looking in the mirror and seeing "normal" and then thinking it's abnormal... it just doesn't compute for me. It's not about normal or abnormal. It's about whether I'm meeting my own standards, whether I'm maintaining the control I need to get through everything I have to do. If I meet those standards, then it's right. If I don't, then it's wrong. Normal doesn't even factor into it.

doctor.intent: determine if patient has a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think your body shape is acceptable to you, regardless of what others say?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When I look at photos from the showcase, I don’t really see the artwork first—I zoom in on my arms and waist, and if I look small enough I feel like I’m serious and put-together.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question asks if the patient finds their body shape acceptable regardless of others' opinions. This directly relates to how the patient evaluates themselves based on their body shape and weight, which matches the Body Image/Weight/Shape Disturbance symptom.

patient.answer:
I mean, acceptable? I guess so, as long as it looks the way I need it to look. Like, it’s not really about what other people think is acceptable, it’s about how I feel when I see myself in certain situations. For example, we just had this big end-of-semester showcase for my advanced seminar—it was this huge event, lots of faculty there, really important for networking and getting cleared for those youth workshops I mentioned earlier. And of course, people were taking a million pictures. 

When my friend sent me the link to the photo album later that night, I was sitting in my dorm, supposed to be finishing up that massive paper, but I just started clicking through the pictures. And the thing is, when I look at photos from the showcase, I don’t really see the artwork first, or who I’m standing with, or even what’s going on in the background. I immediately zoom in on myself. I zoom right in on my arms, on my waist, checking to see how I look in that specific lighting, from that specific angle. 

And if I look small enough in those pictures, if I can see that my arms look lean and my waist looks tight, then I feel... I feel acceptable. I feel like I look serious, like I’m a put-together person who has everything under control and deserves to be taken seriously by those professors. But if I don't see that, if I look even a tiny bit softer or wider than I expect, it just ruins everything. I can't even look at the rest of the picture. So, yeah, it's acceptable to me, but only when it meets that specific criteria I have for myself, because that's what tells me I'm actually doing things right, regardless of whatever everyone else is saying.
